title: US Outposts Were Dangerous Bubbles: How the War on Terror Trapped Itself
dek: US outposts in Afghanistan were meant to protect villages, but became magnets for conflict. The harder they fought, the more bloated and immobile they became, until they were trapped by the fortresses they built.
why: Wesley Morgan served in Afghanistan and spent a decade researching the deep contradictions of the War on Terror: tactical success coexisting with strategic failure. Worth the time of anyone who thinks about war and organizations.
who: Readers interested in military history, US tactics, and organizational behavior, especially those curious about the inside story of the War on Terror and how military decisions get made.

points.h: The outpost became a dangerous bubble
points.body: In the summer of 2010, Wesley Morgan embedded with troops entering the Pech Valley in Afghanistan and found that US outposts, meant to provide security for villages, had actually become ‘dangerous bubbles’ that drew conflict toward the villagers. Both US forces and the enemy suffered few casualties; it was the villages outside the outposts that truly suffered. This contrast led him to ask: who built these outposts, why, and when — questions that ultimately became his book The Hardest Place.

points.h: US forces grew heavier and dumber
points.body: From 2006 to 2010, US forces in eastern Afghanistan gradually lost flexibility and mobility, tethered to heavy outposts and MRAPs. In 2006 the 10th Mountain Division could still reach remote areas by pickup truck and ATV, but by 2010, due to the IED threat and top-down force protection requirements, conventional units could barely reach those places and had to rely on special operations for offensive missions. This overextension meant follow-on units could not sustain the earlier reach.

points.h: Two ODA teams: restraint vs. aggression
points.body: In 2004, two Green Beret ODA teams deployed to the Pech Valley in succession. The first, from the Utah National Guard's 19th Special Forces Group, adopted an ‘ink spot’ approach, trying to build security around the district center and refusing to enter the Korengal Valley because they sensed something there was luring them in. The second, from the 3rd Special Forces Group at Fort Bragg, was eager to get into the Korengal to find a fight, and ended up entangled in a local tribal timber dispute, used as muscle for one faction, starting the Korengal ‘snowball’ that eventually became a fierce battlefield lasting years.

points.h: Three incompatible tribes within the US military
points.body: In eastern Afghanistan, the US military contained three ‘tribes’: conventional forces; the Green Berets (working with local partners such as training Afghan National Army commandos and local police); and the Joint Special Operations Task Force (such as Task Force 373, composed mainly of SEAL Team 6 and Rangers, conducting night raids). These three had different objectives, sometimes supporting each other but more often getting in each other's way. For example, the task force might kill someone conventional forces could have easily arrested, while only the task force could operate in remote areas conventional forces couldn't reach. This lack of coordination was a core problem of the Afghanistan war.

points.h: Commanders measured success with the wrong metrics
points.body: Many commanders lacked real understanding of counterinsurgency and could only rely on quantifiable performance metrics such as ordnance dropped, miles of road built, and number of meetings held. The book gives an example: the 2nd Battalion, 503rd Infantry Regiment, during 15 months of combat in Kunar Province, lost 24 soldiers, and its commander, Lt. Col. Bill Ostland, defined success by the number of JDAMs dropped, ammunition expended, SERP budget spent, and 10,000 Beanie Babies distributed — metrics that could not reflect actual effects and were even self-contradictory.

points.h: Navy admirals with ground combat résumés
points.body: Wesley Morgan points out that many current senior US Navy and Air Force officers have a chapter in their careers completely different from the conventional path: they led Provincial Reconstruction Teams (PRTs) in Afghanistan's Kunar and Nuristan provinces, including submarine officers, nuclear engineers, and naval aviators. For example, the current commander of INDOPACOM, Sam Paparo, led the PRT in Nuristan for a year. These assignments occurred simultaneously with the fighting in Wana and Narisan, and they went out daily in MRAPs on counterinsurgency missions. This experience became a unique mark on their careers.

points.h: Military-media relations went from transparent to hostile
points.body: Morgan recalls that in 2007, as a 19-year-old freelance journalist, he could almost freely choose which unit to embed with, and public affairs just helped him reach company and platoon level units. But today, since the embed system ended in 2013-2014, military-media relations have deteriorated sharply, and a new generation of officers at battalion level and below view the media as something terrifying. He believes the turning point was not the McChrystal affair, but after Obama's second term, when the military began restricting embeds and pushing the war out of sight, because the complicated message that ‘advisors’ were actually ‘combat advisors’ was unwelcome.

points.h: How Multicam became a mark of elite status
points.body: Morgan tells the story of how Multicam camo spread: it was invented around 2002 by a Brooklyn art school graduate, lost the Army's competition (the Army chose the poorly performing ACU camo), but Delta Force adopted Multicam privately because ACU performed badly at night. It then spread through special operations and became a mark of elite status. Crucially, Crye Associates hinted to game producers that this was elite camo, so Multicam appeared in games like Ghost Recon before real photos did, building an elite image in the minds of young soldiers.
